[[File:A-B_testing_example.png|thumb|upright=1.4|Example of A/B testing on a website. Some users (chosen at random) are served a version of the website with a blue button, while others see a version with a green button. From this, the relative efficacy of the two designs can be measured.]]
'''A/B testing''' (also known as '''bucket testing''', '''split-run testing''' or '''split testing''') is a [[user experience|user-experience]] research method.<ref name="Young2014">{{Cite journal |last=Young |first=Scott W. H. |date=August 2014 |title=Improving Library User Experience with A/B Testing: Principles and Process |journal=Weave: Journal of Library User Experience |volume=1 |issue=1 |doi=10.3998/weave.12535642.0001.101 |doi-access=free |hdl-access=free |hdl=2027/spo.12535642.0001.101}}</ref> A/B tests consist of a [[randomized experiment]] that usually involves two variants (A and B),<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Kohavi |first1=Ron |url=https://experimentguide.com/ |title=Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments: A Practical Guide to A/B Testing |last2=Xu |first2=Ya |last3=Tang |first3=Diane |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=2000 |access-date=22 October 2021 |archive-date=22 October 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211022221504/https://experimentguide.com/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite encyclopedia |year=2023 |title=Online Controlled Experiments and A/B Tests |encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of Machine Learning and Data Science |publisher=Springer |url=https://exp-platform.com/encyclopediamldm/ |last1=Kohavi |first1=Ron |editor-last=Phung |editor-first=Dinh |pages=891–892 |doi=10.1007/978-1-4899-7502-7_891-2 |isbn=978-1-4899-7502-7 |last2=Longbotham |first2=Roger |editor2-last=Webb |editor2-first=Geoff |editor3-last=Sammut |editor3-first=Claude |access-date=21 April 2023 |archive-date=21 April 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230421021311/https://exp-platform.com/encyclopediamldm/ |url-status=live |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite magazine |last1=Kohavi |first1=Ron |last2=Thomke |first2=Stefan |date=September–October 2017 |title=The Surprising Power of Online Experiments |url=https://hbr.org/2017/09/the-surprising-power-of-online-experiments |magazine=Harvard Business Review |pages=74–82 |access-date=27 January 2020 |archive-date=14 August 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210814183956/https://hbr.org/2017/09/the-surprising-power-of-online-experiments |url-status=live }}</ref> although the concept can be also extended to multiple variants of the same variable. It includes application of [[statistical hypothesis testing]] or "[[two-sample hypothesis testing]]" as used in the field of [[statistics]]. A/B testing is employed to compare multiple versions of a single [[variable (mathematics)|variable]], for example by testing a subject's response to variant A against variant B, and to determine which of the variants is more effective.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Hanington |first=Jenna |date=12 July 2012 |title=The ABCs of A/B Testing |url=http://www.pardot.com/blog/abcs-ab-testing/ |url-status=deviated |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151224151946/http://www.pardot.com/blog/abcs-ab-testing/ |archive-date=2015-12-24 |access-date=2016-02-21 |website=Pardot |language=en-US}}</ref>

Multivariate testing or multinomial testing is similar to A/B testing but may test more than two versions at the same time or use more controls. Simple A/B tests are not valid for [[observational]], [[quasi-experimental]] or other [[non-experimental]] situations—commonplace with survey data, offline data, and other, more complex phenomena.

== Definition ==
"A/B testing" is a shorthand for a simple randomized [[Controlling for a variable|controlled]] experiment, in which a number of samples (e.g. A and B) of a single [[Multivariate random variable|vector-variable]] are compared.<ref name=Young2014/> A/B tests are widely considered the simplest form of controlled experiment, especially when they only involve two variants. However, by adding more variants to the test, its complexity grows.<ref name=":12">{{cite book |doi=10.1007/978-1-4899-7687-1_891 |chapter=Online Controlled Experiments and A/B Testing |title=Encyclopedia of Machine Learning and Data Mining |year=2017 |last1=Kohavi |first1=Ron |last2=Longbotham |first2=Roger |pages=922–929 |isbn=978-1-4899-7685-7 }}</ref> 

The following example illustrates an A/B test with a single variable:

A company has a customer [[database]] of 2,000 people and launches an email campaign with a discount code in order to generate sales through its website. The company creates two versions of the email with different [[Call to action (marketing)|calls to action]] (the part of the copy that encourages customers to act—in the case of a sales campaign, make a purchase) and identifying promotional codes.

* To 1,000 people, the company sends an email with the call to action stating "Offer ends this Saturday! Use code A1",
* To the remaining 1,000 people, it sends an email with the call to action stating "Offer ends soon! Use code B1".
* All other elements of the emails' copy and layout are identical. 

The company then monitors which campaign has the higher success rate by analyzing the use of the promotional codes. The email using the code A1 has a 5% [[response rate (survey)|response rate]] (50 of the 1,000 people emailed used the code to buy a product), and the email using the code B1 has a 3% response rate (30 of the recipients used the code to buy a product). The company therefore determines that in this instance, the first call to action is more effective and will use it in future sales. A more nuanced approach would involve applying statistical testing to determine whether the differences in response rates between A1 and B1 were [[statistically significant]] (highly likely that the differences are real, repeatable and not the result of random chance).<ref>{{cite web |website=developer.amazon.com |url=https://developer.amazon.com/public/apis/manage/ab-testing/doc/math-behind-ab-testing |title=The Math Behind A/B Testing |access-date=2015-04-12 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150921174256/https://developer.amazon.com/public/apis/manage/ab-testing/doc/math-behind-ab-testing |archive-date=2015-09-21 }}</ref>

In the previous example, the purpose of the test is to determine the more effective strategy for encouraging customers to make a purchase. If, however, the aim of the test had been to determine which email would generate a higher [[click-through rate]] (the percentage of people who actually click the link after receiving the email), the results might have been different.

For example, even though more of the customers receiving the code B1 accessed the website, because the call to action did not state the end date of the promotion, many recipients may feel no urgency to make an immediate purchase. Consequently, if the purpose of the test had been simply to determine which email would bring more traffic to the website, the email containing code B1 might well have been more successful. An A/B test should have a defined, measurable outcome, such as sales converted, clickthrough rate or registration rate.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kohavi |first1=Ron |last2=Longbotham |first2=Roger |last3=Sommerfield |first3=Dan |last4=Henne |first4=Randal M. |title=Controlled experiments on the web: survey and practical guide |journal=Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery |date=February 2009 |volume=18 |issue=1 |pages=140–181 |doi=10.1007/s10618-008-0114-1 |s2cid=17165746 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

== Common test statistics ==
[[Two-sample_hypothesis_testing|Two-sample hypothesis tests]] are appropriate for comparing the two samples in which the samples are divided by the two control cases in the experiment. [[Z-test]]s are appropriate for comparing means under stringent conditions regarding normality and a known standard deviation. [[Student's t-test|Student's ''t''-test]]s are appropriate for comparing means under relaxed conditions when less is assumed. [[Welch's t test|Welch's ''t''-test]] assumes the least and is therefore the most commonly used two-sample [[hypothesis test]] in which the mean of a metric is to be optimized. While the [[mean]] of the variable to be optimized is the most common choice of [[estimator]], others are regularly used.

[[Fisher's exact test]] can be employed to compare two [[binomial distribution]]s, such as a [[click-through rate]].

==Segmentation and targeting==
A/B tests most commonly apply the same variant (e.g., user interface element) with equal probability to all users. However, in some circumstances, responses to variants may be heterogeneous. While a variant A might have a higher response rate overall, variant B may have an even higher response rate within a specific segment of the customer base.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://online-behavior.com/testing/advanced-ab-testing-tactics-1356|title=Advanced A/B Testing Tactics That You Should Know &#124; Testing & Usability|website=Online-behavior.com|access-date=2014-03-18|archive-date=2014-03-19|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140319000032/http://online-behavior.com/testing/advanced-ab-testing-tactics-1356|url-status=dead}}</ref>

For instance, in the above example, the breakdown of the response rates by gender could have been:

{| class="wikitable" style="text-align:right"
|-
! Gender !! Overall !! Men !! Women
|-
! Total sends 
| 2,000 || 1,000 || 1,000
|-
! Total responses 
| 80 || 35 || 45
|-
! Variant A 
| {{sfrac|50 | 1,000}} (5%) || {{sfrac|10 | 500}} (2%) || {{sfrac|40 | 500}} (8%)
|-
! Variant B 
| {{sfrac|30 | 1,000}} (3%) || {{sfrac|25 | 500}} (5%) || {{sfrac|5 | 500}} (1%)
|}

In this case, while variant A attracted a higher overall response rate, variant B actually elicited a higher response rate among men.

As a result, the company might select a segmented strategy as a result of the A/B test, sending variant B to men and variant A to women in the future. In this example, a segmented strategy would yield a 30% increase in expected response rates from <math display="inline">5\% = \frac{40 + 10}{500 + 500}</math>  to <math display="inline">6.5\% = \frac{40 + 25}{500+500}</math>.

If segmented results are expected from the A/B test, the test should be properly designed at the outset to be evenly distributed across key customer attributes, such as gender. The test should contain a [[representative sample]] of men vs. women and assign men and women randomly to each “variant” (variant A vs. variant B). Failure to do so could lead to experiment [[bias]] and inaccurate conclusions.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://drjasondavis.com/2013/09/12/eight-ways-youve-misconfigured-your-ab-test/|title=Eight Ways You've Misconfigured Your A/B Test|date=2013-09-12|website=Dr. Jason Davis|access-date=2014-03-18|archive-date=18 March 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140318224917/http://drjasondavis.com/2013/09/12/eight-ways-youve-misconfigured-your-ab-test/|url-status=live}}{{self-published source|date=August 2024}}</ref>

This segmentation and targeting approach can be further generalized to include multiple customer attributes rather than a single customer attribute{{emdash}}for example, customers' age and gender{{emdash}}to identify more nuanced patterns that may exist in the test results.

== Tradeoffs ==

=== Positives ===
The results of A/B tests are simple to interpret to create a clear picture of real user preferences, as they directly test one option over another. A/B tests can also provide answers to highly specific design questions. One example of this is Google's A/B testing with hyperlink colors. In order to optimize revenue, Google tested dozens of hyperlink hues to determine which colors attract the most clicks.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Statt |first=Nick |date=2016-05-09 |title=Google is experimenting with turning search results from blue to black |url=https://www.theverge.com/2016/5/9/11642926/google-search-results-blue-black-color-link-experiment |access-date=2024-09-25 |website=The Verge |language=en}}</ref> 

=== Negatives ===

A/B tests are sensitive to [[variance]]; they require a large [[sample size]] in order to reduce [[standard error]] and produce a statistically significant result. In applications in which active users are abundant, such as with popular online social-media platforms, obtaining a large  sample size is trivial. In other cases, large sample sizes are obtained by increasing the experiment enrollment period. However, using a technique coined by Microsoft as Controlled Experiment Using Pre-Experiment Data (CUPED), variance from before the experiment start can be taken into account so that fewer samples are required to produce a statistically significant result.<ref>{{Cite conference |last=Deng |first=Alex |date=February 2013 |title=Improving the Sensitivity of Online Controlled Experiments by Utilizing Pre-Experiment Data |conference=WSDM '13: Proceedings of the sixth ACM international conference on Web search and data mining |doi=10.1145/2433396.2433413 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.statsig.com/blog/cuped |title=CUPED Explained |date=18 May 2023 |first=Craig |last=Sexauer |department=Blog |access-date=11 September 2024 |archive-date=4 September 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240904202759/https://www.statsig.com/blog/cuped |url-status=live }}</ref>

Because of its nature as an experiment, running an A/B test introduces the risk of wasted time and resources if the test produces unwanted or unhelpful results.

==History==

It is difficult to definitively establish when A/B testing was first used. The first randomized [[blinded experiment|double-blind]] trial to assess the effectiveness of a [[homeopathy|homeopathic]] drug occurred in 1835.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Stolberg |first1=M |title=Inventing the randomized double-blind trial: the Nuremberg salt test of 1835 |journal=Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine |date=December 2006 |volume=99 |issue=12 |pages=642–643 |doi=10.1177/014107680609901216 |pmid=17139070 |pmc=1676327 }}</ref> Experimentation with [[advertising]] campaigns, which has been compared to modern A/B testing, began in the early 20th century.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.convertize.com/what-is-ab-testing/ |title=What is A/B Testing |website=Convertize |access-date=2020-01-28 |archive-date=17 August 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200817215345/https://www.convertize.com/what-is-ab-testing/ |url-status=live }}</ref> The advertising pioneer [[Claude C. Hopkins|Claude Hopkins]] used promotional [[coupon]]s to test the effectiveness of his campaigns. However, this process, which Hopkins described in his 1923 book ''[[Scientific Advertising]]'', did not incorporate concepts such as [[statistical significance]] and the [[null hypothesis]], which are used in [[statistical hypothesis testing]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.investors.com/news/management/leaders-and-success/claude-hopkins-scientific-advertising-bio/ |title=Claude Hopkins Turned Advertising Into A Science |access-date=2019-11-01 |website=[[Investor's Business Daily]] |date=20 December 2018 |archive-date=10 August 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210810111651/https://www.investors.com/news/management/leaders-and-success/claude-hopkins-scientific-advertising-bio/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Modern statistical methods for assessing the significance of sample data were developed separately in the same period. This work was conducted in 1908 by [[William Sealy Gosset]] when he altered the [[Z-test]] to create [[Student's t-test|Student's ''t''-test]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://blog.gembaacademy.com/2007/06/20/how-beer-influenced-statistics/ |title=How beer influenced statistics |date=20 June 2007 |first=Ron |last=Pereira |work=Gemba Academy |department=Blog |access-date=22 July 2014 |archive-date=5 January 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150105221541/http://blog.gembaacademy.com/2007/06/20/how-beer-influenced-statistics/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Box |first1=Joan Fisher |title=Guinness, Gosset, Fisher, and Small Samples |journal=Statistical Science |date=1987 |volume=2 |issue=1 |pages=45–52 |doi=10.1214/ss/1177013437 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

With the growth of the internet, new ways to sample populations have become available. Google engineers ran their first A/B test in 2000 to determine the optimum number of results to display in its search-engine results.<ref name=":0" /> The first test was unsuccessful because of glitches that resulted from slow loading times. Later A/B testing research was more advanced, but the foundation and underlying principles generally remain the same, and in 2011, Google ran more than 7,000 different A/B tests.<ref name=":0" />

In 2012, a [[Microsoft]] employee working on the search engine [[Microsoft Bing|Bing]] created an experiment to test different methods of displaying advertising headlines. Within hours, the alternative format produced a revenue increase of 12% with no impact on user-experience metrics.<ref name=":1" /> Today, major software companies such as Microsoft and Google each conduct over 10,000 A/B tests annually.<ref name=":1" />

A/B testing has been claimed by some to be a change in philosophy and business-strategy in certain niches, although the approach is identical to a [[between-subjects design]], which is commonly used in a variety of research traditions.<ref name="wired">{{cite web|url=https://www.wired.com/business/2012/04/ff_abtesting/|title=The A/B Test: Inside the Technology That's Changing the Rules of Business|work=Wired Business|last=Christian|first=Brian|date=2000-02-27|access-date=2014-03-18|archive-date=17 March 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140317101247/http://www.wired.com/business/2012/04/ff_abtesting|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://www.wired.com/wiredenterprise/2012/05/test-everything/|title=Test Everything: Notes on the A/B Revolution &#124; Wired Enterprise|last=Christian|first=Brian|magazine=Wired|access-date=2014-03-18|archive-date=16 March 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140316061405/http://www.wired.com/wiredenterprise/2012/05/test-everything|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://boingboing.net/2012/04/26/ab-testing-the-secret-engine.html|title=A/B testing: the secret engine of creation and refinement for the 21st century|author=Cory Doctorow|date=2012-04-26|publisher=Boing Boing|access-date=2014-03-18|archive-date=9 February 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140209001259/http://boingboing.net/2012/04/26/ab-testing-the-secret-engine.html|url-status=live}}</ref> A/B testing as a philosophy of web development brings the field into line with a broader movement toward [[evidence-based practice]].

Many companies now use the "designed experiment" approach to making marketing decisions, with the expectation that relevant sample results can improve positive conversion results.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Marketing Experimentation Explained: Strategy and Best Practices |url=https://amplitude.com/explore/experiment/marketing-experimentation |access-date=2026-03-06 |website=Amplitude |language=en}}</ref> It is an increasingly common practice as the tools and expertise grow in this area.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2020-01-17 |title=A/B Testing: The ABCs of Paid Social Media |url=https://anyword.com/blog/a-b-testing-paid-social-media/ |access-date=2022-04-08 |website=[[Anyword]] |language=en-US |archive-date=31 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220331132522/https://anyword.com/blog/a-b-testing-paid-social-media/ |url-status=live }}</ref> As a result, more marketing teams now use A/B testing to guide decisions, matching the rigor of the test to measured hypotheses and measuring impact on outcomes such as conversions, revenue, and downstream conversion.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Crowell |first=Collin |date=May 16, 2025 |title=Experimentation Is Not One Method |url=https://www.kameleoon.com/blog/experimentation-is-not-one-method |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251214115553/https://www.kameleoon.com/blog/experimentation-is-not-one-method |archive-date=December 14, 2025 |access-date=March 6, 2026 |website=Kameleoon}}</ref>

== Applications ==

=== Social media ===

A/B tests have been used by large [[social media|social-media]] sites such as [[LinkedIn]], [[Facebook]] and [[Instagram]] to understand [[user engagement]] and satisfaction of online features, such as a new feature or product. A/B tests have also been used to conduct complex experiments on subjects such as [[network effect]]s when users are offline, how online services affect user actions and how users influence one another.<ref name=":2">{{cite book |last1=Xu |first1=Ya |last2=Chen |first2=Nanyu |last3=Fernandez |first3=Addrian |last4=Sinno |first4=Omar |last5=Bhasin |first5=Anmol |title=Proceedings of the 21st ACM SIGKDD International Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining |chapter=From Infrastructure to Culture: A/B Testing Challenges in Large Scale Social Networks |date=10 August 2015 |pages=2227–2236 |doi=10.1145/2783258.2788602 |isbn=9781450336642 |s2cid=15847833 }}</ref>

=== E-commerce ===
On an e-commerce website, the [[purchase funnel]] is typically a helpful candidate for A/B testing, as even marginal decreases in [[Conversion tracking|drop-off rates]] can represent a significant gain in sales. Significant improvements can be sometimes seen through testing elements such as copy text, layouts, images and colors.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.webics.com.au/blog/google-adwords/split-testing-guide-for-online-retailers/|title=Split Testing Guide for Online Stores|date=August 27, 2012|publisher=webics.com.au|access-date=2012-08-28|archive-date=3 March 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210303181237/https://www.webics.com.au/blog/google-adwords/split-testing-guide-for-online-retailers/|url-status=live}}</ref> In these tests, users only see one of two versions, as the goal is to discover which of the two versions is preferable.<ref name=":3">{{Cite conference |last1=Kaufman |first1=Emilie |first2=Olivier |last2=Cappé |first3=Aurélien |last3=Garivier |date=2014 |title=On the Complexity of A/B Testing |url=http://proceedings.mlr.press/v35/kaufmann14.pdf |volume=35 |pages=461–481 |book-title=Proceedings of The 27th Conference on Learning Theory |bibcode=2014arXiv1405.3224K |arxiv=1405.3224 |access-date=27 February 2020 |archive-date=7 July 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210707144220/http://proceedings.mlr.press/v35/kaufmann14.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Product pricing ===
A/B testing can be used to determine the right price for a product, which is one of the most difficult challenges faced when a new product or service is launched. A/B testing (especially valid for digital goods) is an effective mechanism to identify the price point that maximizes the total revenue.{{Citation needed|date=June 2025}}

=== Political A/B testing ===
A/B tests have also been used by [[political campaign]]s. In 2007, [[Barack Obama 2008 presidential campaign|Barack Obama's presidential campaign]] used A/B testing to garner online attraction and understand what voters wanted to see from Obama.<ref name=":4">{{Cite book|last1=Siroker|first1=Dan|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VfVvAAAAQBAJ&q=A/B%20Testing&pg=PT13|title=A / B Testing: The Most Powerful Way to Turn Clicks Into Customers|last2=Koomen|first2=Pete|date=2013-08-07|publisher=John Wiley & Sons|isbn=978-1-118-65920-5|access-date=15 October 2020|archive-date=17 August 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210817043106/https://books.google.com/books?id=VfVvAAAAQBAJ&q=A/B%20Testing&pg=PT13|url-status=live}}</ref> For example, Obama's team tested four distinct buttons on their website that led users to register for newsletters. Additionally, the team used six different accompanying images to attract users.<ref name=":4" />

=== HTTP routing and API feature testing ===
[[File:HTTP AB Testing.png|thumb|right|HTTP router with A/B testing]]
A/B testing is commonly employed when deploying a newer version of an API.<ref name="usenex18_one">{{cite conference|conference=LISA 2018|title=Modern HTTP Routing|url=https://www.usenix.org/sites/default/files/conference/protected-files/lisa18_slides_szucs.pdf|first=Sandor|last=Szucs|year=2018|website=Usenix.org|access-date=1 September 2021|archive-date=1 September 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210901185744/https://www.usenix.org/sites/default/files/conference/protected-files/lisa18_slides_szucs.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> For real-time user experience testing, an [[HTTP]] [[OSI model#Layer 7: Application layer|layer 7]] [[reverse proxy]] is configured in such a way that ''n''% of the HTTP [[Network traffic|traffic]] is routed to the newer version of the backend instance, while the remaining ''100-n''% of HTTP traffic hits the (stable) older version of the backend HTTP application service.<ref name="usenex18_one" /> This is usually achieved to [[Traffic shaping|limit]] the exposure of customers to a newer backend instance such that, if there is a bug with the newer version, only ''n''% of the total [[user agent]]s or clients are affected while others are routed to a stable backend, which is a common ingress control mechanism.<ref name="usenex18_one" />
